evidence.label: The joint Dickman law for consecutive integers

headline: The largest prime factors of n and n + 1 act like independent dice, so each wins half the time.
scope: The law holds for fixed powers a and b between 0 and 1, in ordinary counting over all large ranges.
plain: Every whole number has a largest prime factor, and its size follows a known curve called the Dickman law. Erdős and Pomerance asked in 1978 whether neighbours n and n + 1 have independent sizes. This paper proves they do in ordinary counting, with no exceptional ranges (Lean proof listed). So in the limit, n + 1 has the bigger largest prime factor for exactly half of all n.
doesNot: This does not say how fast the shares approach their limits, and it gives no error term.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

visual.title: Proven guaranteed share of n with P⁺(n) < P⁺(n+1)
visual.note: Earlier values are lower bounds on lower density. The paper's 1/2 is an exact limit.

points.who: de la Bretèche, Pomerance and Tenenbaum

explanation:
Take the number 14. Its largest prime factor is 7. A prime is a whole number above 1 with no divisors except 1 and itself. The next number, 15, has largest prime factor 5. So here the first number has the bigger one. Now try 20 and 21. Their largest prime factors are 5 and 7, so the second number wins.

Run this contest for every whole number n from 2 up to one million, against its neighbour n + 1. The neighbour wins 500,148 times out of 999,999. That is about 50.01 percent. It looks like a fair coin. Yet a computer count cannot show that the share settles at exactly one half. Only a proof about all numbers can.

Start with one number at a time. Mathematicians measure the largest prime factor on a logarithmic scale, as a power of the number. A power of 1/2 means the largest prime factor is about the square root. Work beginning with Karl Dickman in 1930 found the long-run share for each power. The answer is given by the Dickman function, a fixed curve. For the square root, the share tends to 1 − ln 2, about 30.7 percent. Up to one million it is still only 26.8 percent. These shares settle slowly.

In 1978, Paul Erdős and Carl Pomerance asked about two neighbours together. Do n and n + 1 behave like two separate dice? If so, a simple prediction follows. Both would have largest prime factor below their square root for about 9.4 percent of numbers. That is 30.7 percent times 30.7 percent. Erdős and Pomerance proved that each winner in the contest has a guaranteed positive share. Their explicit floor was 0.0099. Later work raised it to 0.05544, then 0.1356, then 0.2017. Yang's 2026 preprint gives 0.280 for both orderings. These are only floors. None shows that the share actually settles.

Closer work came from Joni Teräväinen in 2018. He proved the predicted independence for a weighted count. In that count, each number n counts as 1/n, so small numbers weigh more. Terence Tao and Teräväinen then got ordinary counts, but with an exception. Some rare ranges of numbers were left uncovered. Zhiwei Wang got the full ordinary result, but only by assuming an unproved conjecture about primes.

So the one obstacle was ordinary counting at every large range, with no rare bad ranges and no extra assumption. That is the gap this paper closes. It argues by contradiction. Suppose the link between neighbours failed along some sequence of ranges. The paper rewrites n and n + 1 through chosen factors. That turns the link into one between numbers a short distance apart. A known theorem on short stretches of numbers, due to Kaisa Matomäki and Maksym Radziwiłł, then rules it out.

The result is the joint Dickman law. Pick any two powers a and b between 0 and 1. Count the n whose largest prime factor is at most n to the power a. Also require n + 1 to have largest prime factor at most n to the power b. The share of such n tends to the product of the two single shares. In plain terms, the two sizes behave like independent dice. The paper proves this (Lean proof listed).

Now return to the contest. Two independent draws from the same smooth curve almost never tie. Each is equally likely to come first. So the share of n where the neighbour wins tends to exactly one half. The reverse ordering also tends to one half. The theorem guarantees a limit, not a speed. It gives no error term, so it does not say how close one million should be.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the joint law in ordinary counting. Lean has also checked that each ordering has share one half. The paper's other consequences, such as the upper-tail statement of Erdős and Pomerance, are not in the Lean scope note. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Lean checks formal versions of the joint law and the one-half orderings. The paper gives no rate of convergence, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A prime number that divides a given whole number exactly.
The biggest prime dividing a number, written P⁺(n); P⁺(15) = 5.
A fixed curve giving the long-run share of numbers whose largest prime factor is below a given power.
The long-run share of whole numbers with a property, counting every number equally.
A weighted long-run share where each number n counts as 1/n.
A floor the share stays above at every large range, even if the share never settles.
Two quantities are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
